titulo.texto: Morelos and Iturbide: Two Paths to Independence

frase_gancho.texto: One was a muleteer and priest, the other an officer in the king’s army; both were born in Valladolid, and their names became linked.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue ahead to the next stop, where the story moves forward to eighteen forty-seven and the war with the United States, when another foreign army reached this very hill.

guion_corto.texto: José María Morelos was born in Valladolid in seventeen sixty-five. As a young man he worked as a muleteer, then became a priest, and in eighteen ten he joined Miguel Hidalgo. Agustín de Iturbide was also from Valladolid, but he fought on the king’s side. One date connects the two: the twenty-fourth of December, eighteen thirteen, when Iturbide defeated Morelos’s forces. Years later, Iturbide switched sides and allied himself with Vicente Guerrero. On the twenty-seventh of September, eighteen twenty-one, he led the Army of the Three Guarantees into Mexico City. The two are part of the same story, seen from opposite shores.

guion_largo.texto:
Few stories of the Independence show as many twists as that of these two men. According to the National Museum of History, the War of Independence hall covers four stages. They run from Hidalgo’s uprising to the consummation of eighteen twenty-one. Morelos and Iturbide belong to two of them.

Morelos was born on the thirtieth of September, seventeen sixty-five, in Valladolid, today Morelia. His father was a carpenter, and his mother taught him to read. At fourteen he worked with an uncle on a hacienda near Apatzingán, and so he came to know the Tierra Caliente, the setting of his campaigns. Britannica and the National Institute of Historical Studies of the Revolutions of Mexico describe him as a muleteer. In seventeen ninety he entered the San Nicolás College, whose rector was Miguel Hidalgo, and years later he was ordained a priest. By seventeen ninety-nine he was already the parish priest of Carácuaro.

On the twentieth of October, eighteen ten, Hidalgo named him lieutenant to raise the south. Five days later, Morelos left Carácuaro with twenty-five men. That campaign became famous for the siege of Cuautla: the royalist army camped in front of the town on the seventeenth of February, eighteen twelve, and Morelos broke the siege on the second of May. Later he took Oaxaca and Acapulco.

In September of eighteen thirteen, a Congress was installed in Chilpancingo. Morelos presented the Sentiments of the Nation, with twenty-three points. One says that slavery is forever banned, and so is the distinction of castes. Another states that sovereignty comes from the people. Morelos rejected the title of Highness and preferred to be called Servant of the Nation. On the sixth of November, the Congress declared independence, and in October of eighteen fourteen the Constitutional Decree was promulgated in Apatzingán. You have already seen Morelos twice in the [O’Gorman altarpiece](chap_04_retablo_independencia).

The other part of the story is Iturbide. He was a colonel in the royalist army, born in Valladolid, from a family of Basque origin. He took part in the Battle of Monte de las Cruces. On the twenty-fourth of December, eighteen thirteen, when Morelos tried to take Valladolid, Iturbide completed the insurgent defeat. Morelos was captured on the fifth of November, eighteen fifteen, and shot by firing squad on the twenty-second of December in San Cristóbal Ecatepec.

Then came the twist. In December of eighteen twenty, the viceroyalty sent Iturbide to defeat Vicente Guerrero in the south. Instead of fighting, he invited him to talk, and Guerrero joined the new plan. The Plan of Iguala was proclaimed on the twenty-fourth of February, eighteen twenty-one. It proposed three guarantees: an independent monarchy, equality between Creoles and peninsulares, and the preservation of the Catholic religion and of the privileges of the Church. In August, Iturbide signed the Treaties of Córdoba with Juan O’Donojú, and on the twenty-seventh of September the Army of the Three Guarantees entered Mexico City.

The paths of the two men had different endings. Iturbide was crowned emperor on the twenty-first of July, eighteen twenty-two, in the Metropolitan Cathedral. His empire lasted less than a year. Mexico was then the largest country in Spanish America, with about four million six hundred sixty-five thousand square kilometers and about seven million inhabitants, but the treasury was empty. Iturbide clashed with the Congress and imposed a forced levy of forty percent on the value of each house. The property owners were furious, and a verse circulated in the streets: Forty percent you have taxed the Homeland as a burden; for that reason, in its esteem, you have fallen forty percent. Beware, Agustín, beware. Iturbide abdicated on the nineteenth of March, eighteen twenty-three. He returned to Mexico in eighteen twenty-four, was arrested, and was shot by firing squad on the nineteenth of July, in Padilla, Tamaulipas. His memory is still debated: some remember him as the consummator of Independence, others as the soldier who had earlier fought the insurgents.

The museum’s collection includes pieces from the time of the Army of the Three Guarantees. A twenty twenty-one book on the Consummation reproduces images of them. It mentions a flintlock pistol that belonged to Iturbide, a Three Guarantees flag from eighteen twenty-one, and a drum used to announce the Plan of Iguala. At the museum you can ask which of them are on display today.

texto.Morelos: born in Valladolid on September 30, 1765; shot by firing squad on December 22, 1815
texto.Iturbide: royalist officer born in Valladolid; shot by firing squad on July 19, 1824
texto.Key Documents: Sentiments of the Nation, September 1813; Plan of Iguala, February 24, 1821

texto.pregunta: Myth: Morelos tied the kerchief around his head only to protect himself from the sun.
texto.respuesta: Reality: Academic biographies indicate that, apparently, he wore it because of the migraines he suffered, and that he moistened it with alcohol and eucalyptus. Later, the kerchief became part of his image.
